title: QAOA-in-QAOA: solving large-scale MaxCut problems on small quantum machines
abstract_summary: The paper introduces QAOA-in-QAOA (QAOA2), a hierarchical divide-and-conquer method that enables small quantum devices to tackle large-scale MaxCut problems by partitioning the graph, solving subgraphs with QAOA, and merging local solutions via a reformulated MaxCut leveraging Z2 symmetry. The authors prove a 1/2 approximation ratio lower bound and show empirical results on simulated 10-qubit machines solving 2000-node instances that are competitive with classical Goemans–Williamson performance, with better results on denser graphs and when using community-based partitioning.
methodology_description: The authors propose QAOA-in-QAOA (QAOA2), a hierarchical divide-and-conquer scheme to solve large-scale MaxCut instances on quantum devices with far fewer qubits than the problem size. A given graph is partitioned into multiple subgraphs (via random partitioning or community-detection / modularity-based greedy partitioning). Each subgraph (size ≤ available qubits) is solved independently by a local QAOA instance to obtain a local cut assignment xi (and its global sign-flip ¯xi due to Z2 symmetry). The merging step is reformulated analytically as a new MaxCut instance on h meta-nodes (one per subgraph) with edge weights w'_{ij} computed from the local solutions; this meta-MaxCut is then solved (recursively if h exceeds qubit count) using QAOA or other MaxCut solvers to choose, for each subgraph, whether to flip its local solution. Practically, experiments use 1-layer local QAOA (p=1) for subgraphs, gradient-descent optimization of variational parameters, sampling many bitstrings from the trained circuit and selecting best measured bitstring(s). Goemans–Williamson (GW, SDP-based) is used as the primary classical baseline. Extensive synthetic-graph experiments (unweighted/weighted regular and Erd˝os–R´enyi graphs) with varying node counts, degrees, and repetitions are used to evaluate approximation ratio relative to SDP or asymptotic estimates; ablations explore partition method, subgraph size (available qubits), and QAOA depth.
experimental_setup: Simulations performed with PennyLane quantum simulator on small-qubit circuits (experiments typically constrained to n ≤ 10 qubits for QAOA2 local circuits; a 10-qubit simulator was used for large-instance experiments). Classical SDP (GW) solved via CVXPY with SCS. Shots per circuit: 1000. Sampling: 1000 measured bitstrings per optimized circuit run. Local QAOA training iterations T = 20.
experiment_input: Synthetic graph instances generated by the authors: unweighted/weighted d-regular graphs and unweighted/weighted Erd˝os–R´enyi (ER) graphs. Weighted edges: integer weights sampled uniformly from [0,5]. Problem sizes include small graphs (n in {20,40,60,80,100}) for parameter sweeps, and large graphs up to N=2000 with average degree d=100 (e.g., u100r-2000, w100r-2000, u100e-2000, w100e-2000). For each configuration multiple instances were generated (e.g., 5 instances for 2000-vertex experiments; 10 instances for many smaller settings). Partitioning of the graph produced subgraphs of size ≤ available qubits.
experiment_process: 1) Partition the input graph into h subgraphs using either random partitioning or greedy community-detection maximizing modularity. 2) For each subgraph (size ≤ n qubits) run a local QAOA circuit (typically p=1) with initial state |+>^n, alternating UC(γ) and UB(β) unitaries. 3) Optimize QAOA parameters via classical gradient descent (learning rate 0.01) for T = 20 iterations; evaluate expectation values with shots = 1000. 4) Sample 1000 bitstrings from the trained local circuit and select best local assignment xi. 5) Construct the meta-node MaxCut (merging) problem: compute w'_{ij} from local solutions and local cut values Ci(xi); form C'(s) over h binary variables indicating flips. 6) If h ≤ available qubits solve C'(s) with QAOA (or with GW); otherwise apply the same partition-and-solve procedure recursively to C'(s) until size ≤ qubit budget. 7) Merge local solutions according to the meta-solution s to form a global candidate solution and compute cut value. 8) Compare results to GW baseline (SDP-based) and asymptotic theoretical values; report approximation ratios and statistics over multiple instances and seeds.
experiment_output: Primary metric: approximation ratio r_A = C_A / C*, where C_A is cut found by algorithm A and C* is either the SDP optimum from the GW relaxation (C*_{SDP}) or an asymptotic theoretical value (C*_{asymp}) for some regimes. Outputs include per-instance and aggregate approximation ratios (boxplots, means), heatmaps across degree and graph size, ablation comparisons (partition method, qubit count n, QAOA depth p), and demonstration that QAOA2's approximation ratio is ≥ 1/2 (theoretical bound). Baseline: Goemans–Williamson algorithm with SDP rounding.

They specify key hyperparameters (shots, iterations, learning rate), implementation frameworks (PennyLane, CVXPY, NetworkX), and SDP solver settings, enabling replication of experiments on similar simulators. Random seeds and numbers of instances per configuration are reported in the paper's experimental sections and appendix.
key_findings: [speculative] The merging step for divide-and-conquer MaxCut can be reformulated as a new MaxCut instance using the Z2 symmetry of MaxCut (Theorem 1, proven in the paper).

[speculative] QAOA-in-QAOA (QAOA2) is a hierarchical divide-and-conquer scheme that lets small quantum devices (n qubits) be used to address much larger MaxCut instances (N >> n) by solving subgraphs and then merging solutions.
[speculative] The approximation ratio of QAOA2 is provably lower-bounded by 1/2 (Theorem 2, proven in the paper).

[supported] In numerical simulations (classical quantum simulator), QAOA2 with small circuits (≤10 qubits, p=1 for local QAOAs) achieved approximation ratios that are competitive with or slightly better than the Goemans–Williamson (GW) SDP-based algorithm on several 2000-vertex graph instances.

[supported] Empirical results indicate QAOA2 performance is strongly dependent on graph properties and partition strategy: denser subgraphs, larger subgraph sizes (more qubits), and better partitioning (community detection vs random) improve results.
[supported] Using community-detection-based partitioning (greedy modularity maximization) improved QAOA2 performance relative to random partitioning in their simulations.

[speculative] QAOA2 is claimed to be immune to the usual QAOA scalability limit (i.e., linear qubit requirement) because it reduces large problems to smaller subproblems compatible with limited qubit counts.

[speculative] QAOA2 can be embedded with other advanced strategies (better partitioning, adaptive mixers, distributed variational methods) and generalized to other variational algorithms / domains (e.g., chemistry, QNNs).

[supported] In experiments reported in the paper, increasing available qubits for subproblems improved QAOA2 quality (e.g., moving from 8 to 14 qubits increased approximation ratios by notable amounts in tested instances).

[speculative] The authors suggest QAOA2 may attain runtime efficiency advantages over classical GW due to hierarchy and quantum algorithmic components (no runtime experimental validation is provided).
[supported] Ablation experiments show that explicitly optimizing the merging via the reformulated MaxCut is generally better than naive merging (flip/no-flip) in their benchmarks.
results_summary: The paper introduces QAOA-in-QAOA (QAOA2), a hierarchical divide-and-conquer method that partitions a large MaxCut instance into subgraphs small enough for current quantum devices, solves each subproblem with QAOA (or other solvers), and merges local solutions by formulating a higher-level MaxCut over subproblem choices. The authors prove mathematically that the merge can be cast as a MaxCut and that QAOA2 guarantees a cut value at least half the total edge weight (approximation ratio ≥ 1/2). Classical simulations (using a 10-qubit simulator and p=1 local QAOAs) on several 2000-node graph instances show QAOA2 attains approximation ratios comparable to or slightly better than the Goemans–Williamson SDP-based algorithm, with performance improving for denser graphs, larger per-subgraph qubit budgets, and community-detection partitioning.
performance_claims: [supported] On 2000-vertex graphs (examples: unweighted regular degree-100, weighted regular, unweighted and weighted ER with avg degree 100), QAOA2 achieved mean approximation ratios around 0.848–0.887 depending on instance (examples reported: u100r-2000 mean ≈ 0.861 vs GW ≈ 0.859; weighted regular means ≈ 0.848–0.850 vs GW ≈ 0.844–0.853).
[speculative] The method is claimed able to scale to 'tens of thousands' of nodes using NISQ machines via hierarchical repetition (no empirical demonstration at that scale provided).

[supported] In small-to-moderate sized experiments varying graph density and size, QAOA2 achieved e.g. ≈0.9488 on a dense unweighted regular 20-node graph with degree 9 (u9r-20) and ≈0.5836 on a sparse setting u3r-100 (illustrating sensitivity to density/subgraph quality).
[supported] Increasing the per-subgraph qubit budget from 8 to 14 increased the approximation ratio by ~0.06 (example u9r-60) to ~0.1 (example w9r-60) in their simulations.

[supported] Using community-detection partitioning (greedy modularity maximization) produced large improvements in approximation ratio versus random partitioning in weighted ER instances (examples in the supplement showed increases >0.3 in some instances).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper reports simulation-based instances where QAOA2 matches or slightly outperforms the classical GW approximation on some 2000-vertex graphs, but these results are from classical simulation (not physical quantum hardware), measure approximation quality rather than runtime or scaling-of-resources advantages, and no provable or empirical quantum runtime speedup is demonstrated. Thus any claim of quantum advantage is speculative and conditional on future hardware and algorithmic developments.
limitations: QAOA2 requires partitioning the input graph into subgraphs of size ≤ available qubits, so it depends critically on an effective partition strategy (author-stated).
Performance is sensitive to graph properties: denser graphs give much better results than sparse graphs; weighted graphs are harder (author-stated).
Theoretical guarantee is only a 1/2 approximation lower bound, which can be loose in worst-case instances (author-stated).
QAOA2 performance improves with larger subgraph/qubit size and (to a lesser extent) with circuit depth p — performance on small quantum machines is limited (author-stated).
The approach leverages the Z2 symmetry of MaxCut; applicability to problems lacking such symmetry is not established (author-stated/inherent).
[inferred] The hierarchical partition-and-merge procedure can accumulate errors across levels and may degrade solution quality for many levels of recursion.
[inferred] Random partitioning can leave many inter-subgraph edges, harming performance; instance-aware partitioning is required but nontrivial.
[inferred] Experiments are simulations (10-qubit simulator); performance on noisy real NISQ hardware (noise, readout error, decoherence) is not evaluated.
[inferred] The empirical evaluation uses small-depth local QAOA (often p=1) and limited training iterations (e.g., T=20), which may under-represent achievable performance with more resources.
[inferred] Comparison baselines use SDP-relaxation values or asymptotic formulas as proxies for true optima for large N, so empirical advantage claims are dependent on those proxies.
[inferred] The method requires running many independent QAOA trainings (one per subgraph and for merges), which may incur substantial classical/quantum runtime overhead and sample complexity.
[inferred] The reformulation into a merging MaxCut could still be hard when the number of subgraphs h is large and itself requires partitioning; scalability of that step is not fully characterized.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — QAOA-in-QAOA (QAOA2) is a hierarchical divide-and-conquer scheme: partition large graph into subgraphs solvable on small quantum devices, solve each with local QAOA, then merge via a meta-MaxCut on meta-nodes indicating sign flips.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Empirical simulation results (10-qubit local circuits) on synthetic graphs up to 2000 nodes show QAOA2 achieves approximation ratios competitive with Goemans–Williamson (SDP baseline), especially on denser graphs and with community-based partitioning.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — The method is explicitly designed for small NISQ machines (local circuits n ≤ 10 typical), using shallow local QAOA (p=1) and classical optimization/sampling to produce solutions for very large instances.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Merging leverages analytical reformulation using MaxCut's Z2 symmetry to produce a meta-MaxCut; recursion and classical SDP/QAOA solvers are used interchangeably in merging, illustrating a hybrid quantum-classical pipeline.

#idea:quantum-advantage — The authors prove a theoretical lower bound of 1/2 approximation ratio for QAOA2 and report aggregate statistics (boxplots, means) showing performance trends across degree, graph size, partition method, and qubit budget.

#limitation:qubit-count — Experiments are constrained to local circuits of ≤10 qubits (some sweeps to 12–15), so scalability relies on partition quality and recursion rather than larger quantum hardware.
#limitation:simulation-only — All reported empirical results are from PennyLane simulations (no QPU experiments); reported performance may not reflect noise/imperfections of real devices.

#limitation:data-encoding — The approach requires partitioning and explicit local solution sampling and merging; overheads and fidelity of representing global structure via meta-graph weights may limit applicability to certain graph types.
#idea:hybrid-approach — Practical implementation details: p=1 local QAOA with gradient descent (T=20, lr=0.01), 1000 shots and 1000 samples for selection; authors provide code for reproducibility.
